# Stationary simplex caps in the central barycentric region

## Statement

Let `T` be a `d`-simplex, `d>=2`, with vertices `v_0,...,v_d`, and let
`y in T` have barycentric coordinates `lambda_i`. Assume `lambda_i<=1/d` for
every `i`. A proper cut in this note has vertices strictly on both sides
of its boundary. Consider the relative volume of a halfspace through `y`
as a function of its oriented boundary hyperplane.

If such a cap is stationary and contains at least two vertices strictly
on its included side, it has a direction of strictly negative second
variation. Consequently it is not a local minimum. This includes caps
with some other vertices on the boundary. In particular no stationary
cap with at least two strictly positive and two strictly negative vertex
values is a local minimum.

More precisely, the descending direction only needs the two chosen
positive vertices to satisfy `lambda_i,lambda_j<=1/d`; the other
barycentric coordinates need not satisfy this bound.

Thus every proper local minimum in the stated central region strictly
includes exactly one vertex. This is a statement about proper cuts;
constant-volume supporting traces at boundary points are not being called
proper cuts. The result is not a mixed-integer centerpoint theorem.

## 1. A moment inequality and a reciprocal Laplace transform

If `X` has a probability density on `[0,infinity)` that is positive and
log-concave, then

`E[X^2] <= 2(E[X])^2`.                                      (1)

Equality holds only for an exponential density.

Proof. Its survival function `S`, normalized by `S(0)=1`, is log-concave.
For completeness, if `k` is the density, log-concavity makes
`k(t+s)/k(t)` nonincreasing in `t` for each `s>=0`. Therefore
`S(t)/k(t)=integral_0^infinity k(t+s)/k(t) ds` is nonincreasing and the
hazard `k/S` is nondecreasing. Integrating that hazard gives

`S(s+t)<=S(s)S(t)` for `s,t>=0`.

Tonelli and the tail-moment formulas now give

`E[X^2]/2 = integral_0^infinity t S(t)dt
 = integral_0^infinity integral_0^infinity S(s+t)ds dt
 <= (integral_0^infinity S(t)dt)^2 = (E[X])^2`.

If equality holds, the nonnegative continuous integrand
`S(s)S(t)-S(s+t)` has zero integral and thus vanishes everywhere. The
continuous positive solutions of `S(s+t)=S(s)S(t)`, `S(0)=1`, are
`S(t)=exp(-beta t)`; integrability forces `beta>0`. QED.

Now let `h:[0,infinity)->(0,infinity)` be continuous, integrable and
log-concave, with `h(0)=1`. For `c>0`, set

`A(c)=integral_0^infinity exp(-t/c)h(t)dt`,
`phi(c)=A(c)/c`, and `psi(c)=1/phi(c)=c/A(c)`.

Then `psi` is convex, has limit `psi(0+)=1`, and satisfies

`psi(c)>=1  ==>  psi'(c)>0`.                              (2)

Proof. Write `M_r(c)=integral_0^infinity t^r exp(-t/c)h(t)dt`, so
`A=M_0`. Direct differentiation yields

`psi''(c)=[2 M_1(c)^2-M_0(c)M_2(c)]/[c^3 M_0(c)^3] >=0`,    (3)

by (1) applied to the normalized density
`exp(-t/c)h(t)/M_0(c)`. Differentiation is justified by exponential
domination on compact subintervals of `c>0`. The limit at zero follows
from `A(c)/c=integral_0^infinity exp(-s)h(cs)ds` and continuity at zero;
an integrable log-concave function on the halfline is bounded.

If equality holds in (3) at even one value of `c`, the equality case of
(1) implies `h(t)=exp(-alpha t)` on the whole halfline. Its integrability
forces `alpha>0`, and then `psi(c)=1+alpha c` has positive derivative.
Otherwise (3) is strict for every `c>0`. Strict convexity and the limit
`psi(0+)=1` then give

`psi'(c) > [psi(c)-1]/c >=0`

whenever `psi(c)>=1`. This proves (2). QED.

## 2. Exponential coordinates and stationarity

Let `E_0,...,E_d` be independent unit exponentials. A uniform point of
`T` has barycentric coordinates

`U_i=E_i/G`, where `G=sum_i E_i`.

The vector `U` and the scalar `G` are independent, with `G` having gamma
shape `d+1` and scale one. This follows directly by the change of variables
from `(E_i)` to `(G,U)`, whose Jacobian is `G^d`.

An oriented hyperplane through `y` is represented by its affine values
`c_i` at the vertices, with

`sum_i lambda_i c_i=0`.                                  (4)

Its cap probability is

`P(c)=Pr(V>=0)`, where `V=sum_i c_i E_i`.                  (5)

Assume there are at least two strictly positive `c_i` and at least one
strictly negative `c_i`; other coefficients may be zero. The density `f`
of `V` is positive on the real line and log-concave. Log-concavity is the
standard convolution consequence of Prekopa-Leindler applied to the
signed exponential densities; zero coefficients are omitted. The density
is bounded, continuously differentiable, and has exponential tails.
For example, convolve the sum of two positive exponential phases with
one negative phase: the positive-sum density is continuous and has an
integrable bounded weak derivative, and convolution with the one-phase
density makes the resulting derivative continuous. Further convolution
preserves this property.

In a neighborhood of `c`, the cap probability is continuously
differentiable in every coefficient. It is twice differentiable when
only the positive coefficients are varied while other coefficients are
fixed. Its first derivatives have the size-bias formulas

`P_i(c)=f_{V+c_i E_i'}(0)>0`.                            (6)

For `c_i=0`, this means `P_i(c)=f(0)`. One can justify differentiation
without formal delta functions by conditioning on all but the remaining
signed sum; its density is bounded, and exponential moments dominate the
derivatives. The formulas also follow by integrating against smooth
approximations to the step function and taking the dominated limit.

The exact identity

`sum_i P_i(c)=d f(0)`                                   (7)

can be seen using `V=G L(U)`, `L(U)=sum_i c_i U_i`. The density `f_L` is
continuous near zero: zero is an interior projection value, and with at
least three nonzero coefficients the possible zero-value knot does not
cause a density discontinuity. Independence gives
`f(0)=f_L(0) E[1/G]=f_L(0)/d`. On the other hand, shifting every `c_i` by
`s` replaces `L` by `L+s`, so the directional derivative in the all-ones
direction is exactly `f_L(0)`. This proves (7).

Stationarity of `P` under the linear constraint (4) is therefore
equivalent to

`P_i(c)=d f(0) lambda_i` for every `i`.                   (8)

Indeed its gradient must be a scalar multiple of `lambda`, and (7)
determines that scalar. Every local minimum is stationary: a nonzero
vector in the linear hyperplane (4) parameterizes nearby oriented
hyperplanes, and positive rescaling leaves `P` unchanged.

## 3. Exact positive-coordinate Hessian

Fix the current density `f` and, for a new positive scalar `a`, define

`phi(a)=f_{V+aE'}(0)/f(0)`.

This is exactly the transform in section 1 with

`h(t)=f(-t)/f(0)`.

Its hypotheses hold because `f` is positive, log-concave, continuous, and
integrable on the negative halfline. Write `psi=1/phi` as before.

For positive coefficients `c_i,c_j`, the second derivatives of `P` are

`P_ii=2 f(0) phi'(c_i)`,                                 (9)

and, if `c_i!=c_j`,

`P_ij=f(0)[phi(c_i)-phi(c_j)]/(c_i-c_j)`.                 (10)

For equal positive coefficients, (10) means `P_ij=f(0)phi'(c_i)`.

Proof. Size bias twice gives

`P_ii=-2 f'_{V+c_i E'+c_i E''}(0)`,
`P_ij=-f'_{V+c_i E'+c_j E''}(0)` for `i!=j`.

Differentiating `f_{V+aE'}(0)` in `a` while keeping `V` fixed gives
`-f'_{V+aE'+aE''}(0)`, proving (9). For (10), let
`W=V+c_iE'+c_jE''`. The elementary exponential-convolution ODE gives

`c_j f_W'+f_W=f_{V+c_iE'}`,
`c_i f_W'+f_W=f_{V+c_jE''}`.

Subtracting yields (10), with the asserted sign. The limit as the two
positive coefficients approach equality proves the repeated-coefficient
case, or it follows directly from the preceding size-bias formulas.
All densities differentiated here contain at least four positive
exponential phases, so their first derivatives are continuous. QED.

## 4. A strictly descending pair variation

Choose distinct positive vertices `i,j` with
`lambda_i,lambda_j<=1/d`. At a stationary cap, (6) and (8) give

`q_i:=phi(c_i)=d lambda_i<=1`,
`q_j:=phi(c_j)=d lambda_j<=1`.

Consequently `psi(c_i),psi(c_j)>=1`; section 1 proves

`psi'(c_i)>0`, `psi'(c_j)>0`.                             (11)

Choose a vector `w` with only two nonzero coordinates,

`w_i=q_j`, `w_j=-q_i`.

It is feasible because `sum lambda_l w_l=0`. For sufficiently small
positive or negative `t`, `c+tw` has the same strictly positive chosen
coefficients and still represents a proper hyperplane through `y`.
The first variation is zero by stationarity. Equations (9)--(10), and
`phi=1/psi`, give its second variation exactly as

`w^T Hess(P) w
 =2 f(0) q_i^2 q_j^2
   { D_ij psi - psi'(c_i)-psi'(c_j) }`,                 (12)

where `D_ij psi=[psi(c_i)-psi(c_j)]/(c_i-c_j)` for unequal arguments,
and `D_ij psi=psi'(c_i)` for equal arguments.

If, say, `c_i<c_j`, convexity gives `D_ij psi<=psi'(c_j)`.
The braces in (12) are therefore at most `-psi'(c_i)<0`. At equal
arguments they equal `-psi'(c_i)<0` as well. Thus the second variation is
strictly negative. Taylor expansion on this feasible line proves that
the stationary cap is not a local minimum. This proves the theorem.

If there are at least two strictly negative vertex margins as well, and
their barycentric coordinates are also at most `1/d`, apply the same
argument to the complementary cap. Its volume is `1-P`, and its
stationarity is equivalent to that of `P`. It has a strictly negative
second variation, giving a strictly positive second variation of `P`.
Thus a stationary cap with at least two vertices strictly on each side
in the stated central region is a strict saddle: the tangent Hessian
takes both positive and negative values.

## 5. Boundary conventions and limits of the statement

Zero vertex margins cause no omission in the proof. Their exponential
coordinates do not affect `V`, and their first derivatives equal `f(0)`;
if the cap is stationary they have `lambda_i=1/d` by (8). The pair
variation only changes two strictly positive margins and therefore
retains all zero margins throughout.

If the point has a zero barycentric coordinate, no proper cap with at
least two positive margins can be stationary: (8) would require a
strictly positive first derivative to vanish. Supporting halfspaces with
volume zero or one can have constant-volume neighborhoods when `y` is
on the boundary. These are not proper cuts and are not covered by the
local-minimum conclusion.

For `d=1`, a proper cut of an interval already has only one vertex on
each strict side; the multi-vertex question is vacuous. Nothing in this
note replaces a mixed-integer union by its convex hull or asserts that
a mixed-integer global depth minimizer is a simplex.

## 6. Exact ordinary depth in the central region

As a consequence, for a point with all `lambda_i<=1/d`, its normalized
ordinary halfspace depth in `T` is exactly

`min_i d^d product_{j!=i} lambda_j`.                      (13)

Proof. First assume all barycentric coordinates are positive. The mass
of a cap through `y` is continuous in its unit normal, because a
hyperplane has zero simplex volume. The compact unit sphere therefore
gives a minimizing cap. Every such cap is proper, since `y` is interior.
By the theorem, its strictly included vertex set has exactly one member,
say `i`; zero margins at other vertices are permitted.

Write its intercept on the edge from vertex `i` to vertex `j` as
`(1-t_j)v_i+t_j v_j`, where `0<t_j<=1`. The cap is the simplex with
vertex `i` and these `d` edge intercepts, so its relative volume is
`product_{j!=i} t_j`. The boundary passing through `y` is equivalent to

`sum_{j!=i} lambda_j/t_j=1`.

Arithmetic-geometric mean gives

`product t_j=product lambda_j / product(lambda_j/t_j)
 >= d^d product lambda_j`.

Conversely choose `t_j=d lambda_j`. These intercepts lie on the edges
because `lambda_j<=1/d`, their defining hyperplane passes through `y`,
and the cap has exactly the displayed volume. Taking the minimum over
`i` proves (13).

If `y` is on the boundary of `T`, a supporting halfspace through `y`
has relative volume zero. The right side of (13) is also zero: choose
an index different from one with zero barycentric coordinate. Thus the
same formula holds there. For `d=1`, (13) is the elementary interval
formula `min(lambda_0,lambda_1)`, without requiring the Hessian argument.
QED.
